topic: Osteoporosis: bisphosphonate counseling, drug holiday, denosumab rebound
front: Starting weekly alendronate. Key counseling, and what about stopping denosumab?
bottom: Empty stomach, plain water, upright 30 minutes.

bullets.clue: Take with 6–8 oz plain water, 30 minutes before food or other meds.
bullets.treat: Consider a drug holiday after 5 years (oral) or 3 years (IV zoledronic acid) if risk is lower.
bullets.trap: Never stop denosumab without a follow-on drug: rebound vertebral fractures.

back: Empty stomach, plain water, upright 30 minutes. Key clue: Take with 6–8 oz plain water, 30 minutes before food or other meds. Pharmacist move: Consider a drug holiday after 5 years (oral) or 3 years (IV zoledronic acid) if risk is lower. Exam trap: Never stop denosumab without a follow-on drug: rebound vertebral fractures.

diagram.alt: Do and do not. Empty stomach, plain water, upright 30 minutes.

source.recommendation: Endocrine Society 2019/2020 osteoporosis guideline: reassess after 3–5 years of bisphosphonate; drug holiday in low-to-moderate risk; denosumab should not be stopped without subsequent antiresorptive due to rebound vertebral fractures. Alendronate labeling: take with 6–8 oz plain water at least 30 min before first food/drink/medication; remain upright 30 min.

topic: Adrenal insufficiency & steroid stress dosing
front: Addison's patient on hydrocortisone gets the flu with fever. What changes?
bottom: Stress dose: double or triple the oral dose.

bullets.clue: Maintenance hydrocortisone 15–25 mg/day in 2–3 doses; primary AI adds fludrocortisone.
bullets.treat: Vomiting or crisis: hydrocortisone 100 mg IV/IM right away.
bullets.trap: Wear medical alert ID; carry an emergency injection kit.

back: Stress dose: double or triple the oral dose. Key clue: Maintenance hydrocortisone 15–25 mg/day in 2–3 doses; primary AI adds fludrocortisone. Pharmacist move: Vomiting or crisis: hydrocortisone 100 mg IV/IM right away. Exam trap: Wear medical alert ID; carry an emergency injection kit.

diagram.alt: axis diagram for naplex-127

source.recommendation: Endocrine Society 2016 primary adrenal insufficiency guideline: hydrocortisone 15–25 mg/day in 2–3 doses; fludrocortisone for mineralocorticoid deficiency; adjust glucocorticoid dose for illness (stress dosing); hydrocortisone 100 mg IV for adrenal crisis; patient education, steroid emergency card/medical alert, emergency injection kit.

topic: Contraception: CHC contraindications (smoker ≥35, migraine with aura)
front: A 36-year-old who smokes 20 cigarettes a day asks for combined pills. Can you prescribe?
bottom: No: Category 4 for combined hormonal contraception.

bullets.clue: Also Category 4: migraine with aura, BP ≥160/100, <21 days postpartum.
bullets.treat: Offer a progestin-only method, IUD or implant.
bullets.trap: Smoking <15 a day at ≥35 is still Category 3.

back: No: Category 4 for combined hormonal contraception. Key clue: Also Category 4: migraine with aura, BP ≥160/100, <21 days postpartum. Pharmacist move: Offer a progestin-only method, IUD or implant. Exam trap: Smoking <15 a day at ≥35 is still Category 3.

diagram.alt: chips diagram for naplex-128

source.recommendation: CDC US MEC 2024: CHC Category 4 for age ≥35 and smoking ≥15 cigarettes/day, migraine with aura, SBP ≥160 or DBP ≥100, <21 days postpartum; Category 3 for age ≥35 smoking <15/day; progestin-only methods and IUDs generally Category 1–2.

topic: Emergency contraception: LNG vs ulipristal vs Cu-IUD; weight
front: Unprotected sex 4 days ago, BMI 32. Best emergency contraception?
bottom: Copper IUD, or ulipristal if an IUD isn't an option.

bullets.clue: Levonorgestrel 1.5 mg (OTC) works best within 72 hours; may be less effective with BMI ≥30.
bullets.treat: Ulipristal 30 mg (Rx) within 120 hours; the copper IUD within 5 days is most effective.
bullets.trap: After ulipristal, wait 5 days before starting hormonal contraception.

back: Copper IUD, or ulipristal if an IUD isn't an option. Key clue: Levonorgestrel 1.5 mg (OTC) works best within 72 hours; may be less effective with BMI ≥30. Pharmacist move: Ulipristal 30 mg (Rx) within 120 hours; the copper IUD within 5 days is most effective. Exam trap: After ulipristal, wait 5 days before starting hormonal contraception.

diagram.alt: Steps. Copper IUD, or ulipristal if an IUD isn't an option.

source.recommendation: CDC US SPR 2024: Cu-IUD within 5 days most effective EC; ulipristal acetate 30 mg up to 120 h; levonorgestrel 1.5 mg ideally within 72 h; start/resume hormonal contraception no sooner than 5 days after ulipristal; ACOG: LNG and ulipristal may be less effective in obesity, ulipristal or Cu-IUD preferred.

topic: Asthma: ICS-formoterol MART (Track 1) step therapy
front: Adult with mild asthma uses albuterol alone. What does GINA prefer?

bullets.clue: Steps 3–5: maintenance-and-reliever (MART) with budesonide-formoterol.
bullets.treat: SABA-only treatment raises exacerbation and death risk.
bullets.trap: MART uses the same inhaler; don't add a separate SABA as routine reliever.

back: As-needed low-dose ICS-formoterol (Track 1). Key clue: Steps 3–5: maintenance-and-reliever (MART) with budesonide-formoterol. Pharmacist move: SABA-only treatment raises exacerbation and death risk. Exam trap: MART uses the same inhaler; don't add a separate SABA as routine reliever.

diagram.alt: Do and do not. As-needed low-dose ICS-formoterol (Track 1).

source.recommendation: GINA 2026: Track 1 preferred—as-needed low-dose ICS-formoterol at steps 1–2, maintenance-and-reliever therapy (MART) with ICS-formoterol at steps 3–5; SABA-only treatment not recommended for adults/adolescents.

topic: Acute asthma exacerbation: SABA, systemic steroid, magnesium
front: Adult asthma flare, PEF 50%. Treatment, and when does magnesium come in?
bottom: Repeated SABA, oral corticosteroid, controlled oxygen.

bullets.clue: Prednisolone 40–50 mg daily for 5–7 days in adults.
bullets.treat: IV magnesium sulfate in the ED for severe exacerbations not responding.
bullets.trap: Antibiotics aren't routine: no evidence of infection, no benefit.

back: Repeated SABA, oral corticosteroid, controlled oxygen. Key clue: Prednisolone 40–50 mg daily for 5–7 days in adults. Pharmacist move: IV magnesium sulfate in the ED for severe exacerbations not responding. Exam trap: Antibiotics aren't routine: no evidence of infection, no benefit.

diagram.alt: axis diagram for naplex-131

source.recommendation: GINA 2026 exacerbation management: repeated inhaled SABA (or ICS-formoterol per Track 1), controlled oxygen to SpO2 93–95%, oral corticosteroids (prednisolone 40–50 mg/day for 5–7 days in adults), IV magnesium for severe exacerbations not responding; antibiotics not routinely recommended.

topic: COPD: initial LAMA/LABA; ICS when eos ≥300; dupilumab/ensifentrine
front: COPD with frequent exacerbations, eosinophils 350. First maintenance pick?

bullets.clue: Most symptomatic patients start on LAMA/LABA.
bullets.treat: Add ICS when eosinophils ≥300; on triple with eos ≥300 and chronic bronchitis, consider dupilumab.
bullets.trap: LABA/ICS without a LAMA isn't encouraged in COPD.

back: LAMA/LABA plus ICS (triple). Key clue: Most symptomatic patients start on LAMA/LABA. Pharmacist move: Add ICS when eosinophils ≥300; on triple with eos ≥300 and chronic bronchitis, consider dupilumab. Exam trap: LABA/ICS without a LAMA isn't encouraged in COPD.

diagram.alt: Steps. LAMA/LABA plus ICS (triple).

source.recommendation: GOLD 2026: LAMA+LABA initial for groups B and E; LABA+LAMA+ICS for group E with eosinophils ≥300; LABA+ICS not encouraged; dupilumab (or mepolizumab) for persistent exacerbations on triple therapy with eosinophil phenotype; ensifentrine as maintenance option.

topic: COPD exacerbation: prednisone 40 mg ×5 d, antibiotics
front: COPD flare with more purulent sputum and dyspnea. Steroid regimen and antibiotics?

bullets.clue: Short-acting bronchodilators first: SABA with or without SAMA.
bullets.treat: Antibiotics if sputum is purulent plus more dyspnea or volume, or ventilation needed; 5–7 days.
bullets.trap: Longer steroid courses add harm without benefit.

back: Prednisone 40 mg daily for 5 days. Key clue: Short-acting bronchodilators first: SABA with or without SAMA. Pharmacist move: Antibiotics if sputum is purulent plus more dyspnea or volume, or ventilation needed; 5–7 days. Exam trap: Longer steroid courses add harm without benefit.

diagram.alt: Threshold. Prednisone 40 mg daily for 5 days.

source.recommendation: GOLD 2026 exacerbations: short-acting bronchodilators; systemic corticosteroids prednisone 40 mg/day for 5 days; antibiotics for 5–7 days when increased sputum purulence plus increased dyspnea and/or sputum volume, or mechanical ventilation.

topic: CAP outpatient & inpatient empiric regimens
front: Outpatient CAP, healthy 30-year-old, no recent antibiotics. Regimen?

bullets.clue: Alternatives: doxycycline; a macrolide only if pneumococcal resistance <25%.
bullets.treat: Comorbidities: amox/clav or cephalosporin plus macrolide or doxy, or a respiratory FQ.
bullets.trap: Inpatient non-severe: beta-lactam plus macrolide, or respiratory FQ alone.

back: Amoxicillin 1 g three times daily. Key clue: Alternatives: doxycycline; a macrolide only if pneumococcal resistance <25%. Pharmacist move: Comorbidities: amox/clav or cephalosporin plus macrolide or doxy, or a respiratory FQ. Exam trap: Inpatient non-severe: beta-lactam plus macrolide, or respiratory FQ alone.

diagram.alt: Threshold. Amoxicillin 1 g three times daily.

source.recommendation: ATS/IDSA 2019 CAP: outpatient no comorbidities—amoxicillin 1 g TID, doxycycline, or macrolide (if pneumococcal macrolide resistance <25%); with comorbidities—amoxicillin/clavulanate or cephalosporin plus macrolide or doxycycline, or respiratory fluoroquinolone monotherapy; inpatient nonsevere—beta-lactam plus macrolide or respiratory fluoroquinolone.

topic: HAP/VAP MRSA & Pseudomonas coverage
front: VAP, IV antibiotics in the past 90 days. Empiric coverage?

bullets.clue: MRSA: vancomycin or linezolid. Pseudomonas: pip-tazo, cefepime, meropenem or similar.
bullets.treat: Two antipseudomonal agents only with high risk, e.g., recent IV antibiotics or septic shock.
bullets.trap: Treat 7 days for most; de-escalate on cultures.

back: Cover MRSA and Pseudomonas. Key clue: MRSA: vancomycin or linezolid. Pseudomonas: pip-tazo, cefepime, meropenem or similar. Pharmacist move: Two antipseudomonal agents only with high risk, e.g., recent IV antibiotics or septic shock. Exam trap: Treat 7 days for most; de-escalate on cultures.

diagram.alt: chips diagram for naplex-135

source.recommendation: IDSA/ATS 2016 HAP/VAP: empiric MRSA coverage (vancomycin or linezolid) when risk factors (IV antibiotics within 90 days, MRSA prevalence >10–20% or unknown); antipseudomonal beta-lactam; two antipseudomonal agents from different classes for high risk (IV antibiotics within 90 days, septic shock, etc.); 7-day course; de-escalate.

topic: Uncomplicated cystitis: nitrofurantoin, TMP-SMX, fosfomycin
front: Uncomplicated cystitis, CrCl 70. First-line options and durations?

bullets.clue: TMP-SMX DS BID for 3 days if local resistance <20%; fosfomycin 3 g once.
bullets.treat: Avoid nitrofurantoin when CrCl <30 (Beers).
bullets.trap: Fluoroquinolones are reserved, not first-line, for cystitis.

back: Nitrofurantoin 100 mg BID for 5 days. Key clue: TMP-SMX DS BID for 3 days if local resistance <20%; fosfomycin 3 g once. Pharmacist move: Avoid nitrofurantoin when CrCl <30 (Beers). Exam trap: Fluoroquinolones are reserved, not first-line, for cystitis.

diagram.alt: Threshold. Nitrofurantoin 100 mg BID for 5 days.

source.guideline: IDSA 2011 uncomplicated cystitis/pyelo (still current; IDSA 2025 covers cUTI only)
source.recommendation: IDSA/ESCMID 2011 uncomplicated cystitis: nitrofurantoin monohydrate/macrocrystals 100 mg BID × 5 days; TMP-SMX DS BID × 3 days if resistance <20%; fosfomycin 3 g single dose; fluoroquinolones reserved. AGS Beers 2023: avoid nitrofurantoin if CrCl <30.

topic: C. difficile: fidaxomicin vs oral vancomycin; recurrence
front: First episode of C. difficile, non-severe. Preferred drug and dose?

bullets.clue: Alternative: oral vancomycin 125 mg QID for 10 days.
bullets.treat: Stop unnecessary antibiotics and acid suppression when possible.
bullets.trap: Vancomycin must be oral: IV doesn't reach the colon.

back: Fidaxomicin 200 mg BID for 10 days. Key clue: Alternative: oral vancomycin 125 mg QID for 10 days. Pharmacist move: Stop unnecessary antibiotics and acid suppression when possible. Exam trap: Vancomycin must be oral: IV doesn't reach the colon.

diagram.alt: Threshold. Fidaxomicin 200 mg BID for 10 days.

source.recommendation: IDSA/SHEA 2021 CDI focused update: fidaxomicin 200 mg BID × 10 days preferred for initial episode; vancomycin 125 mg orally QID × 10 days acceptable alternative; metronidazole only for nonsevere if others unavailable; fidaxomicin preferred for recurrence.

topic: SSTI: purulent vs nonpurulent; MRSA oral options
front: Abscess drained; MRSA suspected. Oral options, and what about nonpurulent cellulitis?

bullets.clue: Nonpurulent cellulitis is usually strep: cephalexin or penicillin.
bullets.treat: Incision and drainage is the main treatment for abscesses.
bullets.trap: TMP-SMX and doxycycline don't reliably cover strep.

back: Purulent: TMP-SMX or doxycycline. Key clue: Nonpurulent cellulitis is usually strep: cephalexin or penicillin. Pharmacist move: Incision and drainage is the main treatment for abscesses. Exam trap: TMP-SMX and doxycycline don't reliably cover strep.

diagram.alt: Do and do not. Purulent: TMP-SMX or doxycycline.

source.recommendation: IDSA 2014 SSTI: purulent infections—incision and drainage; MRSA oral options TMP-SMX or doxycycline (clindamycin, linezolid alternatives); nonpurulent cellulitis—streptococcal coverage (penicillin, cephalexin, dicloxacillin, clindamycin).

topic: Bacterial meningitis empiric therapy by age + dexamethasone
front: Suspected bacterial meningitis, age 60. Empiric regimen and steroid timing?

bullets.clue: Age >50 adds ampicillin for Listeria; ages 2–50: vancomycin plus ceftriaxone.
bullets.treat: Dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg q6h, 10–20 minutes before or with the first antibiotic.
bullets.trap: Don't delay antibiotics for CT or lumbar puncture.

back: Vancomycin + ceftriaxone + ampicillin + dexamethasone. Key clue: Age >50 adds ampicillin for Listeria; ages 2–50: vancomycin plus ceftriaxone. Pharmacist move: Dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg q6h, 10–20 minutes before or with the first antibiotic. Exam trap: Don't delay antibiotics for CT or lumbar puncture.

diagram.alt: Do and do not. Vancomycin + ceftriaxone + ampicillin + dexamethasone.

source.recommendation: IDSA 2004 bacterial meningitis: ages 2–50 vancomycin plus ceftriaxone or cefotaxime; >50 add ampicillin; dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg q6h for 2–4 days, first dose 10–20 min before or concomitant with first antibiotic; do not delay antibiotics for imaging.

topic: STIs: ceftriaxone 500 mg, doxycycline for chlamydia; syphilis PCN
front: Uncomplicated gonorrhea and chlamydia. Doses?
bottom: Ceftriaxone 500 mg IM once + doxycycline 100 mg BID ×7 days.

bullets.clue: Ceftriaxone 1 g if weight ≥150 kg.
bullets.treat: Pregnancy: azithromycin 1 g once for chlamydia. Early syphilis: benzathine penicillin G 2.4 million units IM once.
bullets.trap: Azithromycin is no longer first-line for chlamydia.

back: Ceftriaxone 500 mg IM once + doxycycline 100 mg BID ×7 days. Key clue: Ceftriaxone 1 g if weight ≥150 kg. Pharmacist move: Pregnancy: azithromycin 1 g once for chlamydia. Early syphilis: benzathine penicillin G 2.4 million units IM once. Exam trap: Azithromycin is no longer first-line for chlamydia.

diagram.alt: Threshold. Ceftriaxone 500 mg IM once + doxycycline 100 mg BID ×7 days.

source.recommendation: CDC STI Treatment Guidelines 2021: gonorrhea ceftriaxone 500 mg IM once (1 g if ≥150 kg); chlamydia doxycycline 100 mg BID × 7 days (azithromycin 1 g alternative; in pregnancy azithromycin 1 g); primary/secondary/early latent syphilis benzathine penicillin G 2.4 million units IM once.

topic: HIV: initial ART (bictegravir/TAF/FTC, dolutegravir) and PrEP options (incl. lenacapavir)
front: New HIV diagnosis. Initial ART pick, and which long-acting PrEP is twice yearly?

bullets.clue: Start ART rapidly, ideally soon after diagnosis.
bullets.treat: Lenacapavir PrEP: subcutaneous every 6 months.
bullets.trap: Dolutegravir/lamivudine isn't for HBV coinfection or high viral load >500,000.

back: Bictegravir/TAF/FTC or a dolutegravir-based regimen. Key clue: Start ART rapidly, ideally soon after diagnosis. Pharmacist move: Lenacapavir PrEP: subcutaneous every 6 months. Exam trap: Dolutegravir/lamivudine isn't for HBV coinfection or high viral load >500,000.

diagram.alt: flow diagram for naplex-141

source.guideline: HHS Adult/Adolescent ARV Guidelines (updated Oct 27, 2026); CDC PrEP 2021 + CDC lenacapavir PrEP MMWR 2025
source.recommendation: HHS Adult and Adolescent ARV Guidelines (current update): recommended initial regimens include bictegravir/TAF/emtricitabine, dolutegravir plus (TAF or TDF)/(FTC or 3TC), dolutegravir/lamivudine except with HIV RNA >500,000, HBV coinfection, or unknown resistance; rapid ART initiation. CDC 2025 MMWR: lenacapavir SC every 6 months for PrEP.

topic: HIV OI prophylaxis thresholds (PJP CD4<200, MAC)
front: HIV with CD4 150. Which prophylaxis, and is MAC prophylaxis needed if ART starts now?

bullets.clue: Toxoplasma prophylaxis at CD4 <100 with positive IgG; TMP-SMX covers both.
bullets.treat: MAC prophylaxis isn't recommended when ART starts immediately.
bullets.trap: Sulfa allergy: dapsone (check G6PD) or atovaquone.

back: PJP: TMP-SMX DS daily (CD4 <200). Key clue: Toxoplasma prophylaxis at CD4 <100 with positive IgG; TMP-SMX covers both. Pharmacist move: MAC prophylaxis isn't recommended when ART starts immediately. Exam trap: Sulfa allergy: dapsone (check G6PD) or atovaquone.

diagram.alt: Threshold. PJP: TMP-SMX DS daily (CD4 <200).

source.recommendation: NIH/CDC/IDSA Adult OI guidelines: PJP prophylaxis CD4 <200 with TMP-SMX (alternatives dapsone [G6PD testing], atovaquone); toxoplasmosis prophylaxis CD4 <100 with positive Toxoplasma IgG; primary MAC prophylaxis not recommended if ART initiated immediately.

topic: Latent/active TB regimens (3HP, 4R; RIPE) and rifampin DDIs
front: Latent TB, and the patient takes apixaban. Which regimen raises a DDI flag?

bullets.clue: 3HP: isoniazid + rifapentine weekly ×12; 4R: rifampin daily ×4 months.
bullets.treat: Rifampin lowers DOACs, warfarin, many ARVs and hormonal contraceptives; if unmanageable, pick another regimen or drug.
bullets.trap: Active TB: RIPE 2 months, then INH/rifampin 4 months; 4-month HPZM is an option.

back: Rifamycin regimens: 3HP and 4R induce CYP3A4. Key clue: 3HP: isoniazid + rifapentine weekly ×12; 4R: rifampin daily ×4 months. Pharmacist move: Rifampin lowers DOACs, warfarin, many ARVs and hormonal contraceptives; if unmanageable, pick another regimen or drug. Exam trap: Active TB: RIPE 2 months, then INH/rifampin 4 months; 4-month HPZM is an option.

diagram.alt: Steps. Rifamycin regimens: 3HP and 4R induce CYP3A4.

source.guideline: CDC/NTA latent TB 2020; ATS/CDC/ERS/IDSA 2025 TB treatment update (4-mo HPZM option)
source.recommendation: CDC/NTCA 2020 LTBI: preferred 3HP (weekly isoniazid + rifapentine × 12 weeks), 4R (daily rifampin × 4 months), 3HR; ATS/CDC/ERS/IDSA 2025 TB treatment update: RIPE (2 months) then INH/RIF (4 months), or 4-month rifapentine-moxifloxacin (HPZM) regimen for eligible patients. Rifampin is a strong CYP3A4 inducer (labeling).

topic: H. pylori: bismuth quadruple first-line, vonoprazan options
front: First H. pylori treatment, no susceptibility data. Preferred regimen?

bullets.clue: PPI + bismuth + tetracycline + metronidazole.
bullets.treat: Vonoprazan-amoxicillin dual therapy is an alternative.
bullets.trap: No clarithromycin triple unless susceptibility is known.

back: Bismuth quadruple for 14 days. Key clue: PPI + bismuth + tetracycline + metronidazole. Pharmacist move: Vonoprazan-amoxicillin dual therapy is an alternative. Exam trap: No clarithromycin triple unless susceptibility is known.

diagram.alt: Threshold. Bismuth quadruple for 14 days.

source.recommendation: ACG 2024 H. pylori guideline: optimized bismuth quadruple therapy for 14 days preferred for treatment-naive patients; vonoprazan-amoxicillin dual (or vonoprazan triple) acceptable when susceptibility unknown; clarithromycin triple only when susceptibility confirmed; test for eradication.

topic: Sepsis: early antibiotics within 1 h, fluids 30 mL/kg, norepinephrine
front: Septic shock in the ED. Antibiotic timing, fluids and first vasopressor?

bullets.clue: At least 30 mL/kg IV crystalloid in the first 3 hours; balanced crystalloids preferred.
bullets.treat: BMI >30: base fluid volume on adjusted or ideal body weight.
bullets.trap: Add vasopressin as norepinephrine needs rise; don't use dopamine.

back: Antibiotics within 1 hour; norepinephrine first. Key clue: At least 30 mL/kg IV crystalloid in the first 3 hours; balanced crystalloids preferred. Pharmacist move: BMI >30: base fluid volume on adjusted or ideal body weight. Exam trap: Add vasopressin as norepinephrine needs rise; don't use dopamine.

diagram.alt: Threshold. Antibiotics within 1 hour; norepinephrine first.

source.recommendation: Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2026: antimicrobials immediately, ideally within 1 h, for possible/probable/definite septic shock and probable sepsis; at least 30 mL/kg IV crystalloid in first 3 h (actual body weight, or adjusted/ideal if BMI >30); balanced crystalloids; norepinephrine first-line over dopamine, epinephrine; add vasopressin with escalating norepinephrine.

topic: Antimicrobial spectrum: anti-Pseudomonal & anti-MRSA agents
front: Which of these covers Pseudomonas: ertapenem, cefepime, ceftriaxone, pip-tazo?

bullets.clue: Also: meropenem, imipenem, ceftazidime, aztreonam, cipro/levofloxacin, aminoglycosides.
bullets.treat: MRSA: vancomycin, linezolid, daptomycin, ceftaroline, TMP-SMX, doxycycline.
bullets.trap: Daptomycin fails in pneumonia: surfactant inactivates it.

back: Cefepime and pip-tazo. Key clue: Also: meropenem, imipenem, ceftazidime, aztreonam, cipro/levofloxacin, aminoglycosides. Pharmacist move: MRSA: vancomycin, linezolid, daptomycin, ceftaroline, TMP-SMX, doxycycline. Exam trap: Daptomycin fails in pneumonia: surfactant inactivates it.

diagram.alt: chips diagram for naplex-146

source.recommendation: IDSA guidance and product labeling (Sanford Guide 2026): antipseudomonal agents include piperacillin-tazobactam, cefepime, ceftazidime, meropenem, imipenem, aztreonam, ciprofloxacin, levofloxacin, aminoglycosides; ertapenem and ceftriaxone lack reliable Pseudomonas activity; daptomycin not indicated for pneumonia (inactivated by surfactant).

topic: Penicillin allergy cross-reactivity & cephalosporin use
front: History of penicillin hives 20 years ago; surgery needs cefazolin. OK?
bottom: Yes: give cefazolin, no testing needed.

bullets.clue: Cross-reactivity is low (~1–2%) and driven by side chains; cefazolin's is unique.
bullets.treat: Low-risk histories can get a direct oral amoxicillin challenge to remove the label.
bullets.trap: Even after penicillin anaphylaxis, a dissimilar-side-chain cephalosporin can be given.

back: Yes: give cefazolin, no testing needed. Key clue: Cross-reactivity is low (~1–2%) and driven by side chains; cefazolin's is unique. Pharmacist move: Low-risk histories can get a direct oral amoxicillin challenge to remove the label. Exam trap: Even after penicillin anaphylaxis, a dissimilar-side-chain cephalosporin can be given.

diagram.alt: flow diagram for naplex-147

source.recommendation: AAAAI/ACAAI 2022 Drug Allergy Practice Parameter: for history of non-anaphylactic penicillin reaction, administer cephalosporins without testing; for penicillin anaphylaxis, suggest non-cross-reactive (dissimilar side chain) cephalosporin without testing; direct oral amoxicillin challenge for low-risk histories.

topic: GERD: PPI timing, step-down; PPI long-term risks
front: GERD on omeprazole: timing, duration, and long-term risks to counsel?
bottom: 30–60 minutes before the first meal; 8-week trial.

bullets.clue: After response, step down to the lowest effective dose or stop.
bullets.treat: Long-term risks: C. difficile, fractures, low B12 and magnesium.
bullets.trap: Don't stop abruptly after long use: taper to limit rebound acid.

back: 30–60 minutes before the first meal; 8-week trial. Key clue: After response, step down to the lowest effective dose or stop. Pharmacist move: Long-term risks: C. difficile, fractures, low B12 and magnesium. Exam trap: Don't stop abruptly after long use: taper to limit rebound acid.

diagram.alt: Do and do not. 30–60 minutes before the first meal; 8-week trial.

source.recommendation: ACG 2022 GERD: 8-week PPI trial taken 30–60 min before meals; attempt discontinuation or lowest effective dose in responders without indication for long-term therapy. PPI labeling: warnings for C. difficile, fractures, hypomagnesemia, vitamin B12 deficiency.

topic: IBD: 5-ASA vs steroids vs biologics
front: Mild-moderate ulcerative colitis vs Crohn's: does mesalamine work for both?

bullets.clue: UC: oral mesalamine ≥2 g/day, plus rectal for distal disease.
bullets.treat: Moderate-severe: biologics or small molecules; steroids only to induce.
bullets.trap: Never use corticosteroids for maintenance.

back: UC yes; Crohn's no. Key clue: UC: oral mesalamine ≥2 g/day, plus rectal for distal disease. Pharmacist move: Moderate-severe: biologics or small molecules; steroids only to induce. Exam trap: Never use corticosteroids for maintenance.

diagram.alt: Steps. UC yes; Crohn's no.

source.recommendation: ACG 2025 UC: oral 5-ASA ≥2 g/day for mild-moderate UC, rectal 5-ASA for proctitis/left-sided; advanced therapies (biologics, JAK inhibitors, S1P modulators) for moderate-severe; corticosteroids for induction, not maintenance. ACG 2025 Crohn's: 5-ASA not recommended for Crohn's disease.

topic: Cirrhosis: SBP prophylaxis, lactulose/rifaximin, nonselective BB
front: Cirrhosis with prior SBP and an episode of hepatic encephalopathy. Drug regimen?

bullets.clue: Lactulose titrated to 2–3 soft stools daily.
bullets.treat: Add rifaximin 550 mg BID after a recurrence; NSBB for varices, but reduce or stop with hypotension or AKI.
bullets.trap: Avoid NSAIDs: renal injury and bleeding.

back: SBP prophylaxis plus lactulose ± rifaximin. Key clue: Lactulose titrated to 2–3 soft stools daily. Pharmacist move: Add rifaximin 550 mg BID after a recurrence; NSBB for varices, but reduce or stop with hypotension or AKI. Exam trap: Avoid NSAIDs: renal injury and bleeding.

diagram.alt: Steps. SBP prophylaxis plus lactulose ± rifaximin.

source.guideline: AASLD 2021 ascites/SBP/HRS; AASLD/EASL 2014 HE; ACG 2026 HE
source.recommendation: AASLD 2021 ascites/SBP/HRS: long-term antibiotic prophylaxis after SBP episode; avoid NSAIDs. AASLD/EASL 2014 HE and ACG 2026 HE: lactulose titrated to 2–3 soft bowel movements daily; add rifaximin for prevention of recurrence. Nonselective beta-blockers (propranolol, nadolol, carvedilol) for variceal prophylaxis.
